claims.text: The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is homogenized.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
FeNiCrMn has previously been characterized mainly for corrosion resistance, with limited study of its mechanical properties.
Uniaxial tensile tests will be conducted under controlled stress or strain conditions.
In situ digital image correlation can capture full-field strain data during tensile testing.
Testing at ambient and elevated temperatures and at multiple controlled strain rates can map the alloy's mechanical response.
Dislocations, slip bands, and deformation twins mediate strain hardening and ductility in FeNiCrMn.
Mechanical loading activates dislocation motion and possibly deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Activated plastic-deformation mechanisms produce spatially heterogeneous strain fields identifiable by in situ DIC.
Dislocation activity, twinning, and strain localization govern the strength and ductility response of FeNiCrMn.
Controlled tensile loading with in situ DIC will reveal distinct slip, twinning, or strain-localization mechanisms.
The identified deformation mechanisms will correlate with variations in strength and ductility across strain rates and temperatures.
Increasing strain rate and temperature will produce measurable variations in local strain distributions.
Increasing strain rate and temperature will produce quantifiable changes in yield strength and ductility.
Similar alloys have existing tensile-strength and elongation data that can serve as a baseline.
The effects may be restricted to strain-rate and temperature ranges over which the FeNiCrMn microstructure remains stable.
Specimen preparation and surface finish may influence the observed deformation patterns.
The cited CoCrFeMnNi alloy has an excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation.
A lack of statistically significant differences in strain localization or mechanical properties correlated with microstructural evolution would falsify the hypothesis.
